reviews.review: The game is really captivating and demonstrates an excelent writing. I couldn't stop playing it and I beat it in one sitting. Recommended to fans of George Orwell (obviously) and Papers, Please.

Not so much a game as a kind of "choose your own adventure" story.  Takes about 5 hours for 1 playthrough, but I'll definitely be going through it a few more times.  Very interesting concept and story and the art style is superb.  Absolutely worth the money.

I thought this was a very interesting, thought-provoking game unlike anything I've played before. It is all narrative, and a story is built around uncovering bits and pieces of data gathered from the "internet" on behalf of a controlling government. I finished the game in about two days (you could probably finish it in about one day), but there are so many different decisions to make throughout the game that I think it's short on purpose so that you play through multiple times to see different outcomes. I thought it was a good commentary on individual privacy and freedoms in society, and the delicate balance of protection over privacy. I would recommend this game to those who enjoy narrative, story-driven games. Not a lot of action, no voice acting, but the music was nice and atmospheric and the game-play was easy to pick-up.

A fun and unique game that you should definitely play. A decent story told in incredible fashion.

That said:
1)  I softlocked after the ending "cutscene" consistently. I thought at first it might be meta-gameplay, but I doubt the devs intend you to ctrl-alt-del out of the game. Annoying but I got to play and see the entirety of the game anyway (I think). Could just be my setup, so no thumbs down on that from me.
2) The co-worker that works alongside you is annoying as heck. This guy needs to be able to be muted or toned down or something. Drag, drop, clear the coworker's comment becomes fairly tedious.
3) This is a drag-and-drop simulator, make no mistake. There are animated graphics and "movies" in the store screenshots, but they are not interactive and only about 30 seconds of the opening scene.

None of these should stop you from playing this game. It was an interesting and fun experience.
Only about 4 hours of gameplay to finish the story, but it's actually weirdly replayable. The soundtrack is phenomenal.

Fun game, I enjoyed the story and the investigative aspects of this game. 

My one complaint is that the story felt a little linear, sure you can investigate different ways to provide slightly varied storylines, but at the end of the day your story will always end the same way. Still, at least for one playthrough it is worth the ride.

Brilliant story driven game, the plot twists and turns giving you surprises around every corner. Turns out its pretty fun spying on people while investigating crimes :)

I would highly recommend however, the game doesnt offer much replay value unless you are interested in gaining all the multiple endings and it is fairly short (completed in around 5 hours and I took my time to read a lot of the unneccesary articles because the story was so damn interesting)

Hands down the best game I have played, the ending really puts you in a thought of current society and survillance system.

This game is well done. It is a story that you're unfolding by taking actions and decisions. You act as an external people to the events, having access to a "big-brother" database about the people involved. Depending on the data you choose as relevant to the case, the story progresses, and can be replayed with some variability.

Good story, nice design and interesting reflexion on how private data could be used.

Orwell is a very intriguing game that lets you jump into the lives of people within a certain group, figure out their pasts, learning about their lives, and get an idea of their way of thinking. If you enjoy a detective-type atmosphere that will leave you wondering if you made the right decisions on more than one occasion, check this game out, because it's right up that alley.

This game is very short but definitely worth the money.  The story is very intriguing, the characters are very developed, and the game takes several twists and turns as you approach the ending.  The content of the game is very thought provoking the entire way through.  It's also extremely relevant in today's world with our abundance of technology and social media.  There are definitely moments you will doubt you're making the right choice and may end up regretting some previous choices when you begin to find out more information but that definitely kept things interesting!  There are also moments you are confident as can be in making a choice to only find out later you shot yourself in the foot badly with it.  Very well executed and the game developers deserve some serious kudos for this!  I really hope this game gets a bigger spotlight put onto it in the future.

A brilliant and somewhat emotional story. Highly recommended for any antiutopia fan.

I want to tell all about this game but that would mean spoiling stuff. Let's say I'd never guess who the culprit is. And yeah, I'll keep an even closer eye on things that get online. You'll be doing that too.

Amazing game. Decent length for the money. Thoroughly enjoyable with a great plot line. Very unique mechanics with a streamlined UI. 10/10

I've never seen a game like this before. The storytelling is fascinating, both the method by which it's told, and the story itself. Not a very long game, it's true, but it doesn't feel rushed either. Manages to create a sense of tension, anticipation, and drama, out of gameplay that is largely about reading large chunks of text.

My only complaint is that I got a little lost towards the end, and wasn't sure how to proceed a couple of times. I got the (a?) "bad ending" because I couldn't figure out how else to progress the final chapter. It gets a little experimental with its mechanics in the final chapter, and it would've been nice to get more practice, or at least explanation, of what was expected of me. Still, fortunately the game has some replay value, so like any good "choose your own adventure" story, I'll get to explore the many different paths and see where they lead.
kept me guessing the whole time. loved it.
XKeyscore Simulator

Very well written!   I loved the conversations between characters and how real the "flow" seemed, it felt like I was snooping on two people talking, not two scripts being presented to me, the typos, corrections, and staggered replies really sold it.   


I very much enjoyed my playthrough, and I'm interested in seeing the other available endings it has to offer as well (seems like there are at least 3).   I do hope new "seasons" come out soon, I'd love another case to review.  


I'd also like a bit more choice in the research, there could be more conflicts of information, and a consequences for uploading meaningless data.   


Overall I really liked it, hope there is more to come.   Worth $10 easily.

Amazing text-based game, akin to a visual novel but with slightly more gameplay elements. It gives a nuanced exploration of surveillance and safety vs. privacy and personal freedom by putting the player directly in charge of surveilling suspected criminals. From there, you make choices that can severely impact the lives of people of The Nation (and the story), and it's up to you to decide whether it was worth it.

You can sense a bit of the devs' bias on the subject, but it's not heavy-handed at all and you still can craft a story according to your own views, or completely contrary if you like. The writing and variety of choices is interesting enough to warrant a few replays (though devs should consider a skip or fast-forward option for the conversations).

Despite the shorter 5th and last episode, all in all it was an extremely well crafted story, with an interesting twist that makes meta-gaming a lot of fun.
A decent game, shame it was so short. I was enjoying it thoroughly until it ended quite abruptly. Don't expect to get more than five hours out of it.
Couldn't stop playing until I got through the story, and found out how much I need to replay it again.

This game is ripped straight from the pages of 1984 from the game's name, to the chapter names ("Memory Hole", "Unperson" and so on), achievements ("2+2=5", "Doublethink" and so on) and overall feel of prying into the lives of the people in this fictional nation run by "The Party" (Serously, not very subtle about the orwellian referencing here!)

And I loved every second of it! It pulls you in rapidly and in less time than it takes for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim to show the first dragon, this thing has you hook. line and sinker as you try to unravel the conspiracy only to find more questions than answers.

And, with things like "Five Eyes" and the "patriot" act - the real world implications are GOD. DAMN. TERRIFYING!

Seriously, If you only buy one game a century, make this the one!
as a citizen of britain i play games for escapism not being reminded of daily life.

This game...

However, you quickly discover that there is no real "free choice" here. This game channels you through the plot with 13% choices to modify things. "[i]For how could you establish even the most obvious fact when there existed no record outside your own memory?[/i]"

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's [i]1984[/i] will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.

I only had a few minor gripes with Orwell that did not take too much away from the story or my immersion. The only real problem that I had with the game was the fact that you had to open each file up to add data to them, rather than just dragging and dropping them onto the character web.

A compelling story with many twists leaves the player hungry for more, available through multiple playthroughs of the game. A second season to Orwell would be very difficult to achieve, due to the ending of the game. I will not go into depth about what this is, as I cannot without spoiling the game.

I strongly reccomend you play through Orwell if you have read the novel [i]1984[/i] or are interested in games with themes of censorship and/or a malleable story.
I wish there were more games like Orwell.   It tries something original, and for the most part suceeds.  Interesting story, choices matter, and over all a very good game.

[i]Orwell[/i] is an episodic thriller involving the vulnerabilities of social media and easy access to critical digital information. You play as an employee of an NSA-like private government cyber-security agency called "Orwell", of course, named after George Orwell, and peep into your suspects' lives as you dig around for information that could tell if they are involved in anything that could put the lives of innocents in peril. The game is completely story-oriented, and at times, even choice-driven. 

[h1]Story:[/h1]

It's a thriller that follows the episode template like the [i]Telltale Games[/i], played as if you're a guy who's logged into his computer. Everything you do, see, or read is like as if you're logged into a computer. The story has a few interesting characters to read about, to peep into their lives and see just how much information you can dig up on them, and see how connected they are altogether. At times, you'll come across plot twists, and other kinds of ways the story could put you off with how you applied your actions by considering what you just saw right then first-hand, i.e., there may be more than meets the eye here. As the story progresses, the story gets deeper and darker, and your decisions will have to be considered more carefully. Sometimes, even the terms or choices given to you are there just to put you off. 

To me, I felt it drained down a bit when the whole plot unfolded, but it was pretty good overall. I haven't played the game extensively yet to see how many endings I could get, but there are indeed multiple endings. I don't dislike the endings that happen to you based on your choices. But the part of the story that you cannot change - the [b]huge[/b] plot twist - well, I didn't like it much. 

But more importantly, this game shows us just how exposed we are to everyone, and just how oblivious people are these days about this fact. It's pretty sci-fi, but who's to know that this could be our reality in a few years, give or take? We're slowly stumbling our way to a more surveilled future in which, you could say, we are going to live in an almost-communist digital world, where every singly word we type in the webs is taken for granted, and smeared on us as if we have anything troublesome to show for it. Hell, we go "Sorry, NSA" at times. So, in a way, we're just enjoying a false form of freedom. I could go into detail with how this is both good and bad, but this is only a game review, so... moving on. 

[h1]Visuals:[/h1]

The game looks like the people in it gave their own photos, and then they just used a heavily modified version of that Prisma app to convert it all to make it look like as it is. It's not bad. But, it kinda takes away the realism of it. I dunno if I could say it sits well with the tone of the game. I don't think it does. But, it's visually appealing. 

[h1]Mechanics & Gameplay:[/h1]

There's very little to no mechanics. Having the whole investigative thing in the game, it surely  calls for implementing the use of the keyboard. The devs could've considered adding search terms and stuff, but sadly, this mechanic wasn't added to the game, and that, too, takes away the realism from the game. Something like, if you can't find something in the game that you're looking for, that's related to a certain character, search the appropriate term up, and find it (like [i]Her Story[/i]). That's what would make it more engaging, because there's no knowing what you could possibly find. Clicking and dragging can get stale. Hopefully, if they make a follow-up to [i]Orwell[/i], they could implement this.

In the sense of gameplay, it's pretty interesting. As you play, you come across multiple choices to make. You're basically making choices constantly. When you have an info that you have the choice of either using it or not, you will probably think of the following:

"Do I drag this information to the profile?"
"[i]Should[/i] I drag this information to the profile?"
"How does this information have an effect?"
"Is this info even worth putting into the files?"

A simple statement that has to do something with the character - you will think it about in a much deeper manner. Because when you do enter something, it gets reflected on the reports, and that could have a cause-and-effect thing going on. The "choices matter" tag on this game is appropriate. And that's the whole point of the game. You, as an investigator, must see to it that everything you do in this works out perfectly in the end, for the people in Orwell, as well as the public.

[h1]Music:[/h1]

The music fits well with the theme of the game, it's sci-fi-y, it gives off the mysterious vibe, and if you see a plot twist, the music suddenly changes to a very tense, "oh damn" type of tone. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

If all you do in a game is walk, then you call it a "walking simulator". This game is that. All you mostly do is click and drag stuff. Which makes it a "clicking simulator". But, it's appropriate, because you can't really do much with a computer other than click and drag and type, can you? 

Funny (lol, not) jokes aside, the premise of the game is solid, and how they elaborate on it, with you as the very thing that gets to use what's given to you against those [b]like[/b] us. Just imagine if this happened ([b][i]*cough*ishappening*cough*[/i][/b]) in real life. The primary focus of the game was definitely the story, and the story only. The replayability of the game relies on the achievements, and the multiple endings present in the game (for most, even trading cards).

I recommend this game to story lovers, I don't recommend this game to those who get bored of simple mechanics, and I recommend you get this game during the sales. I enjoyed the story a lot, but, I wanted more to do than just clicking and dragging. There's a [i]f-i-i-i-ne[/i] grey area between those two, and I'm right smack in the middle of it. But, being a game that focuses entirely on the story, and the kind of message it's trying to interpret to us, I give it a thumbs up.

It's not often a visual novel type of game makes you jump in your seat. I went into this game thinking "oh cool a game about invation of privacy, this should be fun." and left with " I will never say anything negative online again."

Audio 8/10
Story 10/10
Mechanics 9/10

Orwell is a fitting name for this game; the inspiration from 1984 is extremely prominent, but the plotline will still feel fresh to anyone who's a fan of George Orwell's iconic novella. Imagine 1984 from O'Brien's point of view, with the technology we have in today's society, and that's Orwell.

Let me begin by saying that the thing that sets this game apart from others is its unique gameplay. It's incredibly immersive; you could easily really be an investigator with this fictional government, spying on a terrorist organization and accessing all their personal files. Through the "Orwell" interface, you can click between relevant websites that contain information on those you are investigating; phone, chat, and email correspondance (both archived and happening currently) of your suspects; and PC and phone desktops that contain files, photos, and contacts vital to your mission. Anyone who's fond of "Facebook stalking" to see how much information they can gain just by browsing the web will be 
thrilled with this game.

The story progresses by uploading "data chunks," snippets of relative information found through your resources, to the Orwell server, where it is analyzed by your advisor. While you have access to all the information in front of you, the advisor only has access to that which you upload, meaning that the information you give will have a vital impact on the story; contradictory information can be found all over the place. As such, this isn't just a scavenger hunt where you look for information relating to your mission, this is a game of judgment where your gut feeling and deductive skills will impact the outcome of the game. 

There is no voice acting, no action sequences, no cutscenes; only emails. texts, and phone calls you read through to see what's happening in the world of the game. This lack of animation makes it all the more impressive when you're left on the edge of your seat at the end of an episode and must immediately move to the next to find out what happens. The story is extremely well-told.

The story has an interesting message to give to its players. While we all read 1984 and sympathized with Winston as he was persecuted and brainwashed by a totalitarian government that claims that privacy is only an obstacle in the way of public safety, the game challenges this by putting the player in the shoes of an agent of the equivalent Ministry of Love. As you spy your way through these suspected terrorists' files, emails, and personal pages, one can begin to think that, with good intentions, an agency like this could stop attacks before they happen and save lives. It's a valid question in our current social climate, and is posed elegantly through Orwell's gameplay and story.

To give you an idea of how long the game is, the game has 5 "episodes" to it, and I finished the game in a total of 4.5 hours. However, I will be going back to replay it; as I want to see what happens in the game if I make different choices and upload different data chunks. The game definitely has a replay factor that will increase the amount of time played.

All in all, if you're a fan of dystopian/reverse utopian stories, games with unique interfaces, branching storylines that you have control over, and games you can crank out in a day but definitely will want to replay, I'd recommend Orwell to you.

The premise seems interesting, but the game has some really annoying flaws that prevent me from enjoying it. Maybe it gets better later, but I couldn't tolerate it to get further.

The game constantly just wastes your time, it makes you wait through these long "chats" to catch "evidence". So you end up there, waiting, doing nothing, hoping that one day that chat ends and you can pick up the important pieces.

For some reason prevents you from changing your choices, so if you first think one option is right, then you can't choose another option later. For no other reason, than that the game says so.

It's often unclear as to what certain pieces of "evidence" mean, so you pick up a piece of text that the game tells you is important, and it turns out it's trying to save "wonderland" as a person's address which is ludicrous.

When there's conflicting information, the game sometimes just tells you "there's conflicting information somewhere, but I'm not going to tell you where ha ha good luck finding it", and sometimes it just tells you to throw dice and pick between two equally likely possibilities with no ability to change your opinion as you encounter more evidence later.

There's a tutorial fella that interrupts almost every single thing you do in the game for the first 15-30mins mostly just telling you useless things, or otherwise just annoying you, and there seems to be no chat log available for that.

Overall, I don't really get the point of most of this game.

Orwell is a great gem of a game which involves you taking on the role of an 'investigator', hired to snoop on people and submit information you deem important to the security of the ficitonal country known as 'The Nation'. You are given tasks via a handler who is part of the Orwell system and progresses the story as you pass on details. It's not heavy on politics as such but rather is a 'real time' system and more about understanding people.

Its visual style combines blocky/colourful art with the smoothness of an OS which only has one use. You follow leads and drag info onto appropriate files and whatever you choose to submit will further the story. 

This first run took me 4.6 hours but I think there's more to it than how I played. I chose the hard working straight laced investigator who didn't care about personal issues and basically had no qualms putting innocent people behind bars. I get the impression you can play it differently but perhaps only to a certain extent.

I have to get the cons out of the way: 

- In game the 'relationship viewer' (a part of your display) is rather clunky and you can only clumsily navigate it as your list of suspects grow. I think being able to control movement via arrows oer WASD instead of the mouse would help here. Heck even zooming out!

-Conversations appear to lag and so you can see a reply before the previous message is loaded.

- Finding a 'hot tip' or key piece of information prompts your handler to talk to you (text only, there is no audio, which is a shame) and grey out the text you're reading, forcing you to skip or skim their advice. You very often snoop on phone calls or chat conversations and so this is annoying. Thankfully time is not important in this game but it's still immersion breaking.

What I enjoyed was detaching yourself and being something close to a spy but in reality, you're breaking down the walls of cyber security and seeing how easy it is to investigate something for more or less no reason at all. It questions your conscience constantly and that kind of information can be interesting to process.

I really enjoyed this game, despite being so short, for it's immersive role playing aspects and the questions it raises about our technological future. It so wonderfully sucks you in and weaves a story with characters the are finely tuned. So much intrigue and many times you will consider a decision before acting on it. Thats some damn fine game making.

Lots of reading, so bear that in mind.

Definitely deserves some DLC or a big upgrade including voice work.

Fascinating exploration of the question: how fairly can you judge a total stranger just by browsing through their blog posts and social media history, then their emails, then their phone and PC? Do you fall into the trap of leaping to conclusions by dutifully reporting every charged sentence the suspect has ever uttered, or are you able to step back and look for the whole picture before you decide whether someone is really a threat?

A simple interface, basic graphics, subtle audio, but it all creates a compelling feeling that you're prying into the lives of real suspects. And that you just might have tarred and feathered the wrong person with your reckless cherry picking from the fragments of their digital history.

This is a political horror game with a really fucked up story. Full with 1984 vibe with a gameplay similar to "Papers,please". I really like this game due to its comprehensive story-telling. Mutliple choices and endings makes you feel the cruelty of the in-game world.

THIS GAME WAS AMAZING! I have never played a game that had so much reading and yet was so intriguing! it took me 4ish hours to play, all in one sitting, and my eyes were glued to the screen the whole time. AND THE PLOT TWIST AT THE END!!! I rarely enjoy a game so much!
very good game

For a game that was very much like having a desk job at the National Crime Agency, it was actually surprisingly fun! It played out like reading an interactive novel, and the pacing was just right - not making you feel rushed and giving you time to dig into every little detail and piece the story together. Sometimes I longed for a bit more freedom to add information that I felt was relevant, or about targets I wasn't yet allowed to - this felt a little restrictive and ruined the immersion a bit. However, I imagine it would be incredibly complex design-wise to make the gameplay that open, so I can't complain. The story was relatively short, but I think that this was just about the right length. I would definitely be up for more games like this in the future.

This game does not lets you go back to change conflicting information even if the truth comes out at the different time that the first entry. I get it wants to be part of the narrative but that is bullshit. The job of a text-extractor is to update things on the fly and correct them later, then send them up.

[h1] Orwell [/h1] is a very interesting game to say the least. While gameplay wise you just have to pull and drag some text into a box, the story is captivating as well as how you influence it.

[b] Gameplay [/b]: So Orwell is a game where you embody Big Brother or more like a part of it, an essential yet very subjective part. You goal will be to choose and extract informations on people from their websites, social medias and other public informations but also the data inside their cellphone, personal computer, private phone calls and message, crossing the border of privacy. You interfere with the story by choosing what information are revelante or not, making you think about which information you want to upload or not to Orwell (the Big Brother server). Futhermore choosing to upload one information can make others being not uploadable because it has some conflict with it (2 piece of information can say opposite thing, it's up to you to choose which one is legit or not). this will makes you even more careful about it, and that's good because even if I just had to pull and drag some text, I really got tense during some phase of the game. Felt very immersive

[b] Art [/b] : The art for the pictures is a tad special, but I liked it a lot. The interface is well done and very comfortable to browse. 

[b] Musics and sounds [/b] : The music really got me in this game, I first expected not bad but plane music for this game but it's really not the case. I think that the music is a big factor of why I got this tense (in a good way) in that not so tense pull and drag gameplay. When something bad happens (or will happen) I felt like I had to do things faster even if this game never had timer or whatsoever like it and that you have all your time.

[b] Story [/b] : The characters that you will dig in their privacy are fairly good, they all have interesting personality and felt really human. Story wise it's a little predictable but, well you ARE the big brother so you had every pieces to know what will happen but what I want to focus on is how you influense the story. In the gameplay part I said that what you want to focus on is wheter a piece of information is revelant or not, but that's not quite true if you don't want to be controlled by big brother, you are a small part of it but an essential one, and indirectly you are the one who control the police and the media in this game, so instead of contribute to big brother you can do the opposite, to give you some ideas. (This game have multiple endings and variations depending of which pieces of information you upload or not)

[b] Summary [/b] :

Pros : 
- The story and mostly how you influence it
- The music
- Fairly good characters 

Cons :
- Maybe a tad short even with the multiple endings but it is a wonderful game so I can't really blame it

In the end the system works exactly as it should and helps you find the actual perpetrators while freeing the innocent, but then the VILLAIN you've been pursuing the entire time has the gall to suggest that you reward them for their crimes and tear down the system for no good reason except that you too are being survailled, which is spoken as if it's meant to be a great revelation, when really it's just kind of the obvious logical conclusion one would make when working for a mass survaillence program. I ended up wanting to just carry on with my job and arrest the person I'd been after because the system had worked so well and exactly as intended, I couldn't see a reason it HAD to be torn down. Orwell is the tale of an idealistic german teacher and privacy crusader, who once thought that Privacy and Security could go hand on hand, linked and managed by the use of a Glorified Ethics Manual.

Like all nice things, of course that was doomed to fail. Not an oversight, a bug, or any kind of mistake on the system. It was humanity itself that doomed the man's dream to fail...or succed. 

In Orwell, you are that "humanity", a virtual avatar of yourself, selected by the Goverment of "The Nation" to operate this impressive machine, and act as judge and jury (but not executioner, mind you), all in the name of Security and Stability. A game where choices matter, and even the most petty things you decide to inform (or ignore) have consequences to people out there, decides their fate, their lives. I have to say that at first I couldn't grasp this concept. My first play was very pro-Goverment, and by the end of it, I felt good: I improved the Nation, I helped people. 

But if you are going to play, play more than once. Try to change your choices, ignore things and highlight others. With repetition, the characters started growing on me. People I saw as assholes at first were suddenly adquiring new traits I never saw or thought before. And with repetition, I saw how Orwell was fucking the lifes of these people, I saw the tragedy of these little self-contained stories. 

+Interesting plot
+Simple and clean visuals add to the overall theme of the game
+It's good to play a Big Brother Simulator

-Too short for my taste. I spaced each episode a day apart to make it last, but you could easily beat it in a day.
-Some...concepts about how Orwell works in Ep.5 are a bit silly. "Abe's" plan doesn't make much sense, while there are plenty of reasons for following Initiate's plan, or even for following Delacroix's orders. 

Score: 8/10. Would play again.

Orwell is excellent- it treats a serious ethical issue with the maturity and magnatude it deserves while still delivering an enjoyable and compelling experience. This is a narrative driven experience with an overall linear story but one in which choices do matter- the information you choose to provide can save lives, but it can also cause harm and even death to innocent people. The story does fall into heavy cliches at times, but it also manages to deliver meaningful moments.

If you don't like reading and visual novel style stories this is not for you- most of the game involves combing through conversations and webpages looking for pieces of information that the game helpfully highlights. The main story is also quite linear- you proceed through the main story datachunks in a fairly strict order, but you do have some control over the events of the main story based on what side information you provide, as well as the opportunity to open up diffrent side stories affecting the lives of the different characters. It's fairly short, though it's clearly intended to be played several times, approaching various problems differently each time. 

I did encounter a couple of bugs, but nothing game breaking- at one point a vital datachunk didn't get marked properly and in another the game glitched out during a dialogue and got stuck, but restarts fixed the issue each time.

Overall, an excellent game and highly recommended.

Orwell is a futuristic, anti-statist venture into the realm of adventure gaming.

You are the "investigator" who is tasked to spy on, dissect and apprehend enemies of said state.  You have access to anything any "enemy of the state" may have- including their chat sessions, texting, bank accounts and of course, phone calls and internet usage.

If they speak with others... well, now you get the same for them.

It does do a good job of drawing a line for what it takes to protect people (the story is rooted in a terrorist act that killed multiple people) and personal privacy without knowing the whole story as an outsider.   In fact, it draws much of its strength from the latter. So many out-of-context text and email discussions and phone conversations will easily put you on edge.  Lives are at stake for the next attack.  Can you prevent it?

More of an immersive novel than a game, Orwell begins as a smart and thoroughly engaging experience that accurately captures the dilemma of state surveillance: The violation of privacy is bad and comes with risk, but there are still real threats that motivated the imposition of surveillance in the first place. Within this context, the events of Orwell are situated within "The Nation" - a hypothetical highly developed country saddled with all of the assets and burdens of the U.S., France, the U.K. or any similar nation. Osmotic deserves praise here - they tightly and intelligently create a nuanced setting without overburdening the player.

But the success doesn't last.

As the game progresses, Orwell begins to exhibit a grasping take on modern security that feels naive. The moderated presentation that offered a balanced dialectic fades, and the political messaging of the developers becomes increasingly heavy handed and blunt. None of this occurs in a way that is surprising or unique within the context of the public surveillance debate, it is only disappointing that they couldn't have done better.

In terms of technical game mechanics, while Orwell's gameplay is a slick, engrossing and well-crafted experience - the buyer should not expect any replay value outside of a 3-5 hour playthrough.

Leaving a negative review feels somewhat harsh, although within the context of a 91% positive title, it feels appropriate for balance. It is by no means a bad game - only one that fell frustratingly short of its potential.

This turned out to be a far more captivating game than I anticipated. The concept is definitely interesting right from the get-go, you as an investigator in control of a highly-sophisticated surveillance framework, invading privacies left and right. I'll confess and point out right now though, that there are no NSFW stuff to spy on... Which.. Well. [strike]Might be a downer.[/strike]

BUT NEVERTHELESS.

Great game; thought provoking. I thought myself jaded by this genre, to be honest - what with the lengthy texts and the amount of reading to be done. However, the game mechanics was interesting enough to keep me engaged. I began to feel like I needed to continue just to see what would happen next. The best part about this is definitely the multiple branching paths.

It's nice to feel like your decisions actually make a difference this time. Due to the nature of how the surveillance framework operates, you have to be aware of what you flag and upload, as it might determine how your target is perceived. Of course, how they are perceived translates into how they are treated, resulting in radically different outcomes depending on how you decide to treat them. Would you thus be the empathetic guardian angel, the impartial deliverer of justice or the callous manipulator?

Oooh, [b]lovin' it[/b]. Also loved that many of the names of Achievements were references to George Orwell's 1984. Small little aside, sure, but hey, I'm a sucker.

Musically, there're really only like, three tracks. One plays over more or less the entirety of the game, the other's a rather appropriate ominous musical cue... and the last's a punk rock song. Yep. Not much to comment on, not their biggest selling point, that's for certain.

What is their biggest selling point, and one I want to emphasize here: the story.

This is where it gets very subjective, so read this with a gigantic pinch of salt - your mileage may vary.

Also, mild spoilers (no plot information, just overall themes)

[spoiler]To me, the story was especially relevant because I read George Orwell's 1984 before prior to playing this game (it was the reason why I bought the game, admittedly). Not only that, it also showcases how this might be in our modern world today... Making it, to me, in some ways, an updated version of 1984. The story conveys the impact of such surveillance tools, particularly on privacy, and highlights how... removed it can be from the most important element (to me) in any given situation: CONTEXT.

Whether or not this can be reflected in our reality remains debatable - after all, the framework described is sophisticated enough to transcribe voice conversations (going by how YouTube's auto-captions work... I'll say we're not quite there yet). But I think this is a highly relevant game for our time. It might also be even more pertinent today what with the way we readily provide information online (be it voluntary or not).[/spoiler]

All in all, I feel safe to recommend this game at full price. I had incentive to replay it, coming up to a good length of play-time that I feel justifies the price (more so since I bought it at the Summer Sale). If not the full price, then a discount - always the smarter choice as a consumer.

However this, in a sense, it's also a bit of a weakness, but mainly because it was so good I wanted more of it. I wanted it to last longer. As the game is *very* short even though you can replay chapters in order to get different endings.

Some side activity, some "intermission" missions where you solve different cases, more sudden events, maybe during the main investigation you find evidence of other crimes. 

I understand that creating these fictional lifes is a lot of work so I see the point on remaining laser focused on the main plot. 

But god I really wanted more.
